name: Thermocatalytic Sebaceous Ignition Lance TSIL-1 'Waxwork'
description:
The TSIL-1 projects a narrow infrared beam tuned to the absorption frequency of sebaceous lipids — the fatty compounds produced by skin glands and present in a thin layer across virtually all exposed biological skin. At sufficient power density, the beam flash-heats this lipid layer to ignition temperature within approximately 0.8 seconds of contact, causing the skin's own oils to combust in a thin, intensely hot surface fire. The burn is shallow but severe, covering whatever area of skin was exposed to the beam. The weapon does not penetrate clothing effectively, making exposed skin — face, hands, neck — the primary vulnerable surface.

The TSIL-1's operational signature is distinctive and deeply unsettling: targets ignite seemingly from the inside out, the fire appearing to originate from the skin itself rather than from any visible external source. The psychological effect on witnesses and adjacent targets is pronounced. Ringo Corponation developed the weapon under a cosmetic-technology research umbrella — the original project involved precision lipid-layer treatments for dermatological applications — before the directed-energy weapons division acquired the underlying emitter technology and repurposed it. The cosmetic origin of the technology is something Ringo's PR division works continuously to suppress.

The weapon's range limitation — effective only to about 20 meters before beam dispersion reduces power density below ignition threshold — and its complete ineffectiveness against covered skin have defined its tactical niche as a close-to-mid-range terror and compliance weapon. The nickname 'Waxwork' refers both to the waxy appearance of healed sebaceous burns and to the way targets move in the moments after ignition — arms extended, stumbling, in a manner observers have described as resembling animated wax figures.
specifications: effective range: 2–20 meters power source: High-output infrared emitter cell, 30 shots per charge ignition dwell time: 0.8 seconds on exposed skin burn depth: Superficial to partial-thickness; rarely subcutaneous weight: 1.6 kg form factor: Slim lance profile, one-handed operation, integrated beam focus dial clothing penetration: Negligible through standard fabric; thin synthetic materials may partially transmit augmentation note: Synthetic skin overlays and dermal plating provide full immunity; unaugmented targets are fully vulnerable
tactical_use: The TSIL-1 is used primarily in close-quarters crowd control and targeted suppression, where its psychological impact is as valuable as its physical effect. Security forces use it to drive crowds, create chokepoints, or force individuals to cover — the instinctive reaction to being ignited is to stop, drop, and cover exposed skin, which halts aggression effectively. In one-on-one engagements, operators target the face and hands to immediately degrade the target's fighting capacity. The weapon's licensing status means it appears in the inventories of private security firms, certain licensed bounty hunters, and upscale personal protection details.
cultural_context: The TSIL-1's cosmetic-technology origin is a persistent source of dark humor in GLMZ — 'Ringo made a skin care product that sets you on fire' is a recurring punchline in the city's underground media. The weapon's licensing status, which makes it technically legal for certain operators, has generated significant controversy: advocacy groups argue that a weapon that causes burns to the face cannot be classified as non-lethal regardless of tissue depth. Ringo Corponation has lobbied successfully twice to maintain its licensed status by funding burn treatment research at public hospitals, a gesture widely described as calculated cynicism. Among high-society protection details, carrying a TSIL-1 is considered a mark of refinement — it implies the operator is expected to deter rather than kill.
known_users: Ringo Corponation's own internal security division
story_hooks: Ringo Corponation's original cosmetic-technology research files have surfaced on the grey market, and they describe a higher-powered variant of the TSIL technology capable of full-thickness burns — a variant that was supposedly never manufactured.

A licensed security firm has been using TSIL-1s in a residential district to clear unhoused individuals from a development site. Three people have been hospitalized. Someone needs to document it before the evidence disappears.

A batch of TSIL-1 units has been modified to bypass the 0.8-second ignition delay, achieving near-instant ignition at the cost of reduced range. The modification suggests a specific workshop, and that workshop is connected to something larger.

A Ringo Corponation lobbyist who shepherded the TSIL-1's licensing approval has quietly started carrying one herself. She's scared of something, and whatever it is, she doesn't think a conventional firearm will stop it.

physical_description.visual_profile: A sleek, tapered directed-energy weapon resembling a precision surgical instrument crossed with a futuristic sidearm. The body tapers from a broad grip section to a narrow, almost delicate emitter head, giving it an unexpectedly elegant silhouette despite its cruel function. The overall impression is clinical and cold — something designed in a laboratory rather than a foundry.
physical_description.dimensions: 48 cm overall length, 8 cm grip width, 3.5 cm depth at emitter head. The narrow barrel-like emitter section extends 12 cm from the forward grip, tapering to a 1.2 cm diameter focusing aperture.
physical_description.weight_description: Surprisingly light and balanced — approximately 1.6 kg distributed to favor forward handling. The grip-to-emitter weight ratio feels naturally pointer, encouraging precision aim rather than brute control.
physical_description.primary_material: Aerospace-grade polymer composite body with embedded copper heat-dissipation matrix visible through translucent panels. The emitter head is matte black titanium-alloy shroud housing the infrared optics.
physical_description.finish: Deep matte black polymer with brushed titanium accents around the emitter aperture. Subtle iridescent oil-slick finish on the transparent heat-sink windows reveals internal radiator fins. Minimal weathering in field use, though older units show faint stress marks around the charging port.
physical_description.color_scheme: Primary black with gunmetal grey heat-sink panels and barely-visible RGB status indicators (amber/red) nested beneath the grip. The emitter lens has a faint violet-tinted protective cover.
physical_description.grip_texture: Textured polymer with subtle finger-tracking grooves. Slightly tacky, rubberized feel that aids precision control. The grip surface has microscopic etching to aid sweat and oil resistance — ironic given the weapon's function.
distinctive_features: Integrated beam-focus dial at 2 o'clock position on grip — rotating knurled knob with 1-20m range markings etched in minimal relief
Transparent side panels revealing copper serpentine heat-dissipation tubes running the length of the frame
Slim RGB status LED array (3 lights) nested under the grip near the trigger guard — indicates charge status and thermal state
Charging socket recessed on the rear grip, protected by spring-loaded titanium cover
Precision aperture at emitter head with internal optical focusing lens visible as slight purple tint
Minimal ergonomic finger-grooves, suggesting this is a weapon for precise placement rather than sustained handling
Hairline etching around the emitter head showing thermal stress patterns from repeated use
physical_description.manufacturer_markings: Small RingoFuel corporate sigil (stylized 'R' with fuel-drop motif) laser-etched on the right side of the grip. Serial number and certification stamps embossed on the charging port cover in tiny, precise characters. Regulatory compliance markings appear on the left side near the grip — Tier 3+ licensing identifier.
physical_description.condition_typical: Well-maintained, often showing signs of professional service and careful handling. The delicate optics and precision components mean most field units appear almost clinical in their cleanliness. Veteran units may show micro-scarring on the aperture cover from repeated deployment, or faint heat-stress discoloration around the emitter head. The weapon's prestige status means owners keep it in working condition — visible neglect is rare.
